headline: Hormuz Count Stays Below Normal In Next Traffic Test
deck: Reuters put Thursday transits at seven against a 15-vessel average, while a UKMTO chart independently points to a similar single-digit day with a different count.
body: The physical fact is still a count, not a barrel-loss number: Reuters reported preliminary ship-tracking data showing seven vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, down from 11 the prior day and against a 10-day average of 15. That is the only assigned source row and it carries the useful unit, vessels per day, while leaving vessel class, cargo and deadweight tonnage outside the record. The forecast is that the next visible daily Hormuz transit count for Friday, 11 September 2026, remains below 15 vessels. [E1]

A second domain does not clone the Reuters method, and that matters. A sensor-supplied UKMTO report for 11 September plots 10 September at about four AIS-derived inbound and two outbound Hormuz transits, or six total, while also carrying internally inconsistent date-range labeling elsewhere in the report. That corroborates a sub-15 traffic day without making the Kpler seven-vessel count identical across sources. [E2]

My probability on the next visible count is 64 percent, because both records point to a single-digit prior reading and neither record yet shows a return to the 15-vessel average. The other reading is that the low count was a short AIS snapshot, a reporting-method mismatch, or a one-day routing pause rather than a durable constraint on actual oil and gas movement. The plain fact that would break the call is a Friday, 11 September daily transit count at 15 or higher, or a vessel-class ledger showing normal tanker movement despite the headline count. [E1] [E2]

Tonnage stays outside the call. A seven-ship day is not the same thing as seven laden crude or LNG carriers, and the supplied record does not identify hull classes, cargoes, ballast status or deadweight. That absence keeps the physical conclusion narrow: the visible count was impaired, while total hydrocarbon throughput remains unproved. [E1]

UKMTO's six-count chart helps with corroboration but also keeps the uncertainty alive. Its AIS-derived inbound and outbound bars are close enough to Reuters' seven to support a below-average traffic read, yet the report's own range label means it should not be treated as a completed 11 September count. The next check is therefore a dated traffic-count test, not a claim that the strait has closed or that Gulf export volumes have already fallen. [E2]

What will still matter after the next price tick is the vessel ledger. If the next visible Friday count posts below 15, the low-traffic condition has lasted into a second reading and the probability call holds; if it prints 15 or above, this becomes a one-day disruption story with no demonstrated tonnage loss. Until vessel classes or loading notices arrive, the strongest supported sentence is simply that Hormuz traffic was running below its recent visible norm. [E1] [E2]

evidence_box.fragment: Preliminary ship-tracking data cited by Reuters showed only seven vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, down from 11 the day before and versus a 10-day average of 15.

UKMTO's 11 Sep report plots 10 Sep at about 4 AIS-derived inbound plus 2 outbound Hormuz transits, or 6 total, corroborating sub-15 traffic but differing from Kpler's 7; the report elsewhere labels its range through 9 Sep.
